youtube.baslik: Central Vestibular Disorders and Stroke Warning Signs | Lesson 210 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
When does dizziness come from the brain? In this lesson we cover central vestibular disorders, posterior circulation stroke, the features of central nystagmus (direction-changing with gaze, pure vertical, not suppressed by fixation), and the stroke warning signs that call for urgent physician assessment.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management; Kattah et al., HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome, Stroke (2009); Strupp et al., Acute unilateral vestibulopathy/vestibular neuritis: Diagnostic criteria, Journal of Vestibular Research (2022).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Posterior circulation stroke and warning signs
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about the central causes of dizziness and the most dangerous of them, posterior circulation stroke.
We will cover the features of central nystagmus and the warning signs that call for urgent physician assessment.
In central vestibular disorders, the problem is not in the inner ear or vestibular nerve but in the brainstem, cerebellum or higher.
The vestibular nerve reaches the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, at the border of the pons and medulla.
These nuclei connect with the nuclei that control eye movements through the medial longitudinal fasciculus, or MLF.
The cerebellum is the tuning center of the vestibular system; suppressing nystagmus and holding gaze steady depend largely on it.
A problem anywhere along these pathways can cause dizziness, unsteadiness and particular forms of nystagmus.
Because the central pathways lie close together, dizziness is often accompanied by other neurological symptoms.
But a small lesion, especially in the cerebellum, can also present with dizziness and unsteadiness alone.
Among the central causes of dizziness, the most important in terms of urgency are vascular ones.
Posterior circulation stroke and transient ischemic attack, or TIA, lead the central causes of sudden-onset dizziness.
Multiple sclerosis can cause vertigo through brainstem or cerebellar involvement, especially in young adults.
Degenerative diseases that affect the cerebellum can cause slowly progressive unsteadiness and persistent nystagmus.
Tumors in the posterior fossa and structural problems at the junction of the skull base and spine can also cause central signs.
As we saw in the vestibular migraine lesson, central-type nystagmus can also appear during vestibular migraine attacks.
Some drugs and alcohol can also affect cerebellar function, causing gaze-evoked nystagmus and unsteadiness.
The vessels supplying the brainstem, cerebellum and back of the brain are called the posterior circulation, or vertebrobasilar system.
The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery; the cerebellum is supplied by branches of this system.
Posterior circulation strokes make up about one in five ischemic strokes.
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery, or PICA, strokes can affect the lateral medulla and the lower cerebellum.
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery, or AICA, supplies the lateral pons and often the inner ear.
So in an AICA stroke, sudden hearing loss can accompany vertigo, and the picture can be confused with labyrinthitis.
A small cerebellar stroke can present with acute vertigo and unsteadiness alone, closely mimicking vestibular neuritis.
The classic picture of PICA or vertebral artery occlusion is lateral medullary syndrome, or Wallenberg syndrome.
Vertigo, nystagmus and a tendency to fall toward the lesion side may come with facial numbness on the same side.
Hoarseness, difficulty swallowing and hiccups may also be seen in this picture.
Reduced pain and temperature sensation on the opposite side of the body is a typical finding.
These signs are not always obvious, so in a person with dizziness, ask about facial sensation and swallowing as well.
Brief attacks of vertigo may occur in the days or weeks before a posterior circulation stroke.
These attacks may be transient ischemic attacks, and sometimes dizziness is the only symptom.
Older age, high blood pressure, diabetes and heart rhythm disorders are vascular risk factors.
New attacks of vertigo in a person with one of these risk factors need particular attention.
In a young person, vertigo with new neck pain or headache may suggest vertebral artery dissection.
A dissection is a tear in the inner layer of the vessel wall; it sometimes follows a blow to the neck or a sudden neck movement.
Vertigo that comes with sudden hearing loss also needs urgent assessment for a vascular cause.
Eye findings are the strongest bedside clues for telling peripheral and central vestibular disorders apart.
Peripheral nystagmus beats in one direction; central nystagmus may change direction with the direction of gaze.
Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal and torsional; pure vertical or pure torsional nystagmus is a central sign.
Peripheral nystagmus decreases markedly with visual fixation; central nystagmus may not.
In acute continuous dizziness, the head impulse test is abnormal in peripheral loss but stays normal in most strokes.
Skew deviation, a vertical misalignment of the eyes, is a central sign.
In acute peripheral loss the person can usually walk with help; being unable to stand even with help suggests a central cause.
We covered these principles in detail in the lesson on HINTS: head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew.
Downbeating nystagmus most often arises when the part of the cerebellum that tunes eye movements is affected.
Structural problems at the junction of the skull base and spine, and some drugs, can also cause downbeating nystagmus.
Upbeating nystagmus suggests lesions in the brainstem or the cerebellar midline.
Pure torsional nystagmus is linked especially to lesions in the medulla.
Involvement of the MLF leads to a finding called internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
On side gaze, one eye cannot turn inward, and the eye turning outward shows nystagmus; in a young adult it may suggest multiple sclerosis.
All these findings suggest a central problem and are passed to the physician without delay.
A purely example case: a sixty eight year old with high blood pressure comes in with continuous dizziness that began suddenly this morning.
Hearing is normal; at first glance the picture looks like vestibular neuritis.
But the nystagmus beats right on right gaze and left on left gaze.
The head impulse test is normal in both directions, and the person cannot stand even with help.
Each of these findings suggests a central cause; testing is stopped and the person is referred urgently for a physician's assessment.
This example shows that, in this setting, normal hearing and a normal head impulse test are not reassuring.
Some findings that come with dizziness call for urgent physician assessment for stroke.
New double vision is at the top of this list.
Slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and hoarseness also suggest brainstem involvement.
Numbness and weakness of the face, arm or leg, and clumsiness of hand and arm movements, are also warning signs.
Being unable to stand even with help, or unable to hold the trunk upright when sitting, is a sign of severe imbalance.
New, severe headache or neck pain raises the possibility of arterial dissection, especially in young people.
Sudden hearing loss with acute vertigo also needs urgent assessment for an AICA stroke.

sahneler.baslik: What to do if there is *a warning sign*
cumleler: If any warning sign is present, do not try to finish the planned test battery; testing stops at that moment.
The person is kept in a safe position, protected from falling, and not left alone.
Note the time the symptoms began, or when the person was last seen well.
Using the institution's emergency referral pathway, the person is referred for urgent physician assessment without losing time.
Some stroke treatments can only be given in the first hours, so every minute counts.
The observed nystagmus, head impulse finding and other signs are passed to the team in a short, clear written summary.
Posterior circulation stroke can present with dizziness and unsteadiness alone, which makes it easy to confuse with a peripheral problem.
Some of these people have no obvious neurological signs such as weakness or speech problems.
Diffusion MRI in the first hours may not show some small brainstem and cerebellar strokes.
Young age does not exclude stroke; vertebral artery dissection also occurs in young adults.
A clinician who focuses only on the ear may skip assessing the eye findings and walking.
So in acute dizziness, eye movements, walking and hearing are always assessed together.

sahneler.metin: In acute dizziness, refer urgently to a physician without delay if there is a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, or inability to stand.
cumleler: A tip from the field: do not assess a person with acute, continuous dizziness as if they only had an ear problem.
Always check the direction of the nystagmus, its change with gaze, skew deviation, and whether the person can stand.
If one of these findings suggests a central cause, or there is a warning sign, stop testing and make an urgent referral.
Doubt is reason enough to ask for urgent assessment; an unnecessary referral is always better than a missed stroke.

maddeler.metin: The problem is in the _brainstem_ or cerebellum

cumleler: In central vestibular disorders, the problem lies in the brainstem, the cerebellum or higher pathways.
Posterior circulation stroke, especially a small cerebellar stroke, can present with vertigo alone and mimic vestibular neuritis.
Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, is pure vertical or pure torsional, or is not reduced by fixation suggests a central cause.
Double vision, speech or swallowing problems, numbness, weakness and inability to stand need urgent physician assessment.

sahneler.aciklama: Pure vertical nystagmus, such as _pure downbeating_ nystagmus, is a central sign.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a person with acute dizziness, which nystagmus finding suggests a central cause?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: pure downbeating nystagmus.
The other options fit a peripheral pattern; pure vertical nystagmus suggests a cerebellar or brainstem problem.
